# Values and copying

In robjc, the `RSScalar` family wraps individual R values, while the `RSVector` family wraps R vectors.
An Array, by comparison, holds robjc objects as its elements.
After choosing a wrapper, you need to know whether `copy()` and `mutableCopy()` create a new object and whether they also copy its contents.

This guide uses actual instances to examine how values are wrapped and which references are shared after copying.
For collection lookup and mutation, see the [Collections Guide](guide_07_Collections.Rmd).

## Wrap a single value

For an R value of length one, use a type-specific entry point such as `RSNumber$new()` or `RSString_withValue()` when you know its type.
Use `RSScalar_withValue()` when you want the input type to determine the class.
Raw bytes are outside the `RSScalar` hierarchy; use `RSRaw_withValue()` for them.
Retrieve the wrapped value with `value()`.

```{r}
library(robjc)

direct <- RSNumber$new(3L)
typed  <- RSNumber_withValue(3L)
chosen <- RSScalar_withValue(3L)

stopifnot(direct$isMemberOf(RSNumber))
stopifnot(typed$isMemberOf(RSNumber))
stopifnot(chosen$isMemberOf(RSNumber))
stopifnot(identical(chosen$value(), 3L))

label <- RSScalar_withValue("ready")
stopifnot(label$isMemberOf(RSString))
stopifnot(identical(label$value(), "ready"))
```

These are **separate instances** that hold values.
Even when they wrap the same value, their identities are a separate question.
Use `isEqual()` to compare values, and `identical()` or robjc's `==` to check whether two references point to the same instance.
See the [Identity, Equality, and Hashing Guide](guide_08_Hash_isEqual.Rmd) for details.

If a custom type needs validation or specialized behavior, define a scalar class with `RSScalarClass()`.
The [Class Factory Guide](guide_05_ClassFactory.Rmd) covers its arguments and the creation of NA subclasses.

## Distinguish `NULL` from typed `NA`

In R, `NULL` represents the absence of a value, whereas `NA` is a missing value with a type.
robjc treats them as different objects too.
`RSScalar_withValue(NULL)` returns the shared `RSNull$null` object. A typed NA returns the corresponding scalar class's shared NA instance.

```{r}
stopifnot(identical(RSScalar_withValue(NULL), RSNull$null))
stopifnot(is.null(RSNull$null$value()))

stopifnot(identical(RSNumber$new(NA_integer_), RSNumber$na))
stopifnot(identical(RSScalar_withValue(NA_character_), RSString$na))
stopifnot(is.na(RSString$na$value()))
stopifnot(!identical(RSNull$null, RSString$na))
```

`RSNumber` handles both integers and doubles.
The `value()` of its shared NA instance is `NA_real_`.
You cannot recover whether the original missing R value was an integer or a double from that shared instance.
`RSFactor` is an exception: it does not always collapse missing factors into one NA instance, so their levels and ordering can be retained.
The [scalar technical note](tech_06_Scalars.Rmd) outlines the class cluster implementation.

To **store null as an element** in a collection, explicitly pass `RSNull$null` instead of R's `NULL`.
In a Dictionary, this distinguishes a stored `RSNull` from the R `NULL` returned when a key is absent.

```{r}
fields <- RSMutableDictionary$new()
key <- RSString$new("optional")
fields$setObjectForKey(RSNull$null, key)

stopifnot(identical(fields$objectForKey(key), RSNull$null))
stopifnot(is.null(fields$objectForKey(RSString$new("absent"))))
```

## Wrap a vector

`RSVector` and `RSMutableVector` wrap an R atomic vector as one robjc object.
`RSVector` is the read-only parent; `RSMutableVector` inherits its read and comparison methods and adds mutation methods.
They do not convert each element into an `RSNumber` or another scalar object.
Use `asVector()` to retrieve an ordinary R vector, and `valueAtIndex()` to read a value at a one-based position.
Missing values remain in the vector.

```{r}
values <- RSVector$new(c(10L, NA_integer_, 30L))
stopifnot(identical(values$asVector(), c(10L, NA_integer_, 30L)))
stopifnot(is.na(values$valueAtIndex(2L)))

editable_values <- RSMutableVector$new(c(1L, 2L))
editable_values$appendValues(3L)
stopifnot(identical(editable_values$asVector(), c(1L, 2L, 3L)))
```

Use a Vector when the data naturally forms one R vector, such as a sequence of numbers or strings.
Use an Array when you need to hold individual robjc objects, possibly from different classes.

```{r}
objects <- RSArray_withObjects(list(
  RSNumber$new(10L),
  RSString$new("ten")
))
stopifnot(objects$objectAtIndex(1L)$isMemberOf(RSNumber))
stopifnot(objects$objectAtIndex(2L)$isMemberOf(RSString))
```

## Copy mutable and read-only objects

For Collections and Vectors, `copy()` returns a read-only object and `mutableCopy()` returns an editable one.
Copying a mutable object creates a new outer instance.
Calling `copy()` on a read-only object returns that same instance.

| Receiver | `copy()` | `mutableCopy()` |
|:--|:--|:--|
| Mutable | A separate read-only instance | A separate mutable instance |
| Read-only | The same instance | A separate mutable instance |

```{r}
editable <- RSMutableVector$new(c(1L, 2L))
snapshot <- editable$copy()
another_editable <- snapshot$mutableCopy()

stopifnot(snapshot$isMemberOf(RSVector))
stopifnot(!identical(snapshot, editable))
stopifnot(identical(snapshot$copy(), snapshot))
stopifnot(another_editable$isMemberOf(RSMutableVector))
stopifnot(!identical(another_editable, snapshot))

editable$appendValues(3L)
stopifnot(identical(snapshot$asVector(), c(1L, 2L)))
```

Copies of Collections such as Arrays are **shallow copies**.
Even when the outer Collections are separate, they can share the robjc objects they contain.
In the following example, `saved` and `items` are different Arrays, but both return the same `member`.

```{r}
member <- RSMutableVector$new(c(1L, 2L))
items <- RSMutableArray$new(list(member))
saved <- items$copy()

stopifnot(!identical(saved, items))
stopifnot(identical(saved$objectAtIndex(1L), member))
member$appendValues(3L)
stopifnot(identical(
  saved$objectAtIndex(1L)$asVector(), c(1L, 2L, 3L)
))
```

If the contained objects must also be independent, you need to design how each element is copied.

## Define copying in a custom class

The base class `RSObject` returns `self` from `copy()`.
If your class holds mutable state and needs an independent copy, override `copy()`.
Choose which state to pass to the new instance and run the same validation used in normal construction to help preserve the class's invariants.

```{r}
TagList <- RSObjectClass(
  "Guide06TagList",
  private = list(.tags = NULL),
  public = list(
    initialize = function(tags = character()) {
      super$initialize()
      if (!is.character(tags) || anyNA(tags))
        stop("`tags` must be a character vector without missing values.")
      private$.tags <- tags
      invisible(self)
    },
    tags = function() private$.tags,
    addTag = function(tag) {
      if (!is.character(tag) || length(tag) != 1L || is.na(tag))
        stop("`tag` must be one non-missing string.")
      private$.tags <- c(private$.tags, tag)
      invisible(self)
    },
    copy = function() TagList$new(private$.tags)
  )
)

original <- TagList$new("draft")
duplicate <- original$copy()
stopifnot(!identical(original, duplicate))
stopifnot(identical(original$tags(), duplicate$tags()))

duplicate$addTag("reviewed")
stopifnot(identical(original$tags(), "draft"))
stopifnot(identical(duplicate$tags(), c("draft", "reviewed")))
```

This `copy()` creates a new `TagList` and passes it the original tag values.
R character vectors separate on modification, so adding a tag to the copy does not change the original tags.
For a class that stores another robjc object in a private field, you must decide whether to share that reference or copy the contained object as well.

Use `identical()` to confirm that the copy is a separate instance.
If the two copies should be **equal as values**, define `isEqual()` separately.
When using them in a Set or Dictionary, make `hash()` consistent with that equality.
See the [Identity, Equality, and Hashing Guide](guide_08_Hash_isEqual.Rmd) for details.
